Even the smallest leaf of the believer should be full of the sap of the Holy Spirit (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.7">Jr 17:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">8</reference>). However, the latter reading seems likely to have crept in from <reference osisRef="Eph.6.22">Ep 6:22</reference>. Onesimus--</hi>the slave mentioned in the Epistle to Philemon (Phm 10, 16), "a brother beloved."<div eID="gen36540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a faithful ... brother--</hi>rather, "the faithful brother," he being known to the Colossians as the slave of Philemon, their fellow townsman and fellow Christian.<div eID="gen36541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one of you--</hi>belonging to your city.<div eID="gen36542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">They shall make known unto you all things--</hi>Greek, "all the things here." entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17911"/><div sID="gen36544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17911"/><hi type="bold">10. Aristarchus--</hi>a Macedonian of Thessalonica (<reference osisRef="Acts.27.2">Ac 27:2</reference>), who was dragged into the theater at Ephesus, during the tumult with Gaius, they being "Paul's companions in travel." He accompanied Paul to Asia (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.4">Ac 20:4</reference>), and subsequently (<reference osisRef="Acts.27.2">Ac 27:2</reference>) to Rome. He was now at Rome with Paul (compare Phm 23, 24). As he is here spoken of as Paul's "fellow prisoner," but in Phm 24 as Paul's "fellow laborer"; and vice versa, Epaphras in Phm 23, as his "fellow prisoner," but here (<reference osisRef="Col.1.7">Col 1:7</reference>) "fellow servant," Meyer in Alford, conjectures that Paul's friends voluntarily shared his imprisonment by turns, Aristarchus being his fellow prisoner when he wrote to the Colossians, Epaphras when he wrote to Philemon. The Greek for "fellow prisoner" is literally, fellow captive, an image from prisoners taken in warfare, Christians being "fellow soldiers" (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.25">Php 2:25</reference>; Phm 2), whose warfare is "the good fight of faith."<div eID="gen36544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Mark--</hi>John Mark (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.12">Ac 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.25">25</reference>); the Evangelist according to tradition.<div eID="gen36545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sister's son--</hi>rather, "cousin," or "kinsman to Barnabas"; the latter being the better known is introduced to designate Mark. The relationship naturally accounts for Barnabas' selection of Mark as his companion when otherwise qualified; and also for Mark's mother's house at Jerusalem being the place of resort of Christians there (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.12">Ac 12:12</reference>). The family belonged to Cyprus (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.36">Ac 4:36</reference>); this accounts for Barnabas' choice of Cyprus as the first station on their journey (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.4">Ac 13:4</reference>), and for Mark's accompanying them readily so far, it being the country of his family; and for Paul's rejecting him at the second journey for not having gone further than Perga, in Pamphylia, but having gone thence home to his mother at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.37">Mt 10:37</reference>) on the first journey (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.13">Ac 13:13</reference>).<div eID="gen36546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">touching whom--</hi>namely, Mark.<div eID="gen36547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye received commandments--</hi>possibly before the writing of this Epistle; or the "commandments" were verbal by Tychicus, and accompanying this letter, since the past tense was used by the ancients (where we use the present) in relation to the time which it would be when the letter was read by the Colossians. Thus (Phm 19), "I have written," for "I write." The substance of them was, "If he come unto you, receive him." Paul's rejection of him on his second missionary journey, because he had turned back at Perga on the first journey (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.13">Ac 13:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.37-Acts.15.39">15:37-39</reference>), had caused an alienation between himself and Barnabas. Christian love soon healed the breach; for here he implies his restored confidence in Mark, makes honorable allusion to Barnabas, and desires that those at Colosse who had regarded Mark in consequence of that past error with suspicion, should now "receive" him with kindness. Colosse is only about one hundred ten miles from Perga, and less than twenty from the confines of Pisidia, through which province Paul and Barnabas preached on their return during the same journey. Hence, though Paul had not personally visited the Colossian Church, they knew of the past unfaithfulness of Mark; and needed this recommendation of him, after the temporary cloud on him, so as to receive him, now that he was about to visit them as an evangelist. Again, in Paul's last imprisonment, he, for the last time, speaks of Mark (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">2Ti 4:11</reference>). <div eID="gen36548" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 10. Aristarchus-- a Macedonian of Thessalonica ( Ac 27:2 ), who was dragged into the theater at Ephesus, during the tumult with Gaius, they being "Paul's companions in travel." He accompanied Paul to Asia ( Ac 20:4 ), and subsequently ( Ac 27:2 ) to Rome. He was now at Rome with Paul (compare Phm 23, 24). As he is here spoken of as Paul's "fellow prisoner," but in Phm 24 as Paul's "fellow laborer"; and vice versa, Epaphras in Phm 23, as his "fellow prisoner," but here ( Col 1:7 ) "fellow servant," Meyer in Alford, conjectures that Paul's friends voluntarily shared his imprisonment by turns, Aristarchus being his fellow prisoner when he wrote to the Colossians, Epaphras when he wrote to Philemon. The Greek for "fellow prisoner" is literally, fellow captive, an image from prisoners taken in warfare, Christians being "fellow soldiers" ( Php 2:25 ; Phm 2), whose warfare is "the good fight of faith." Mark-- John Mark ( Ac 12:12 , 25 ); the Evangelist according to tradition. sister's son-- rather, "cousin," or "kinsman to Barnabas"; the latter being the better known is introduced to designate Mark. The relationship naturally accounts for Barnabas' selection of Mark as his companion when otherwise qualified; and also for Mark's mother's house at Jerusalem being the place of resort of Christians there ( Ac 12:12 ). The family belonged to Cyprus ( Ac 4:36 ); this accounts for Barnabas' choice of Cyprus as the first station on their journey ( Ac 13:4 ), and for Mark's accompanying them readily so far, it being the country of his family; and for Paul's rejecting him at the second journey for not having gone further than Perga, in Pamphylia, but having gone thence home to his mother at Jerusalem ( Mt 10:37 ) on the first journey ( Ac 13:13 ). touching whom-- namely, Mark. ye received commandments-- possibly before the writing of this Epistle; or the "commandments" were verbal by Tychicus, and accompanying this letter, since the past tense was used by the ancients (where we use the present) in relation to the time which it would be when the letter was read by the Colossians. Thus (Phm 19), "I have written," for "I write." The substance of them was, "If he come unto you, receive him." Paul's rejection of him on his second missionary journey, because he had turned back at Perga on the first journey ( Ac 13:13 ; 15:37-39 ), had caused an alienation between himself and Barnabas. Christian love soon healed the breach; for here he implies his restored confidence in Mark, makes honorable allusion to Barnabas, and desires that those at Colosse who had regarded Mark in consequence of that past error with suspicion, should now "receive" him with kindness. Colosse is only about one hundred ten miles from Perga, and less than twenty from the confines of Pisidia, through which province Paul and Barnabas preached on their return during the same journey. Again, in Paul's last imprisonment, he, for the last time, speaks of Mark ( 2Ti 4:11 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17915"/><div sID="gen36561" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17915"/>14. It is conjectured that Luke "the beloved physician" (the same as the Evangelist), may have first become connected with Paul in professionally attending on him in the sickness under which he labored in Phrygia and Galatia (in which latter place he was detained by sickness), in the early part of that journey wherein Luke first is found in his company (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.10">Ac 16:10</reference>; compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>). Thus the allusion to his medical profession is appropriate in writing to men of Phrygia. Luke ministered to Paul in his last imprisonment (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">2Ti 4:11</reference>).<div eID="gen36561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36562" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Demas--</hi>included among his "fellow laborers" (Phm 24), but afterwards a deserter from him through love of this world (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2Ti 4:10</reference>). He alone has here no honorable or descriptive epithet attached to his name. Perhaps, already, his real character was betraying itself. <div eID="gen36562" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17917"/><div sID="gen36565" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17917"/><hi type="bold">16. the epistle from Laodicea--</hi>namely, the Epistle which I wrote to the Laodiceans, and which you will get from them on applying to them. Not the Epistle to the Ephesians. See Introduction to Ephesians and Introduction to Colossians. The Epistles from the apostles were publicly read in the church assemblies. Ignatius [Epistle to the Ephesians, 12], Polycarp [Epistle to the Philippians, 3.11,12], Clement [Epistle to the Corinthians, 1. 47], <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.27">1Th 5:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.3">Re 1:3</reference>, "Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear." Thus, they and the Gospels were put on a level with the Old Testament, which was similarly read (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.11">De 31:11</reference>). The Holy Spirit inspired Paul to write, besides those extant, other Epistles which He saw necessary for that day, and for particular churches; and which were not so for the Church of all ages and places. It is possible that as the Epistle to the Colossians was to be read for the edification of other churches besides that of Colosse; so the Epistle to the Ephesians was to be read in various churches besides Ephesus, and that Laodicea was the last of such churches before Colosse, whence he might designate the Epistle to the Ephesians here as "the Epistle from Laodicea." But it is equally possible that the Epistle meant was one to the Laodiceans themselves. <div eID="gen36565" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17918"/><div sID="gen36566" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17918"/><hi type="bold">17. say to Archippus--</hi>The Colossians (not merely the clergy, but the laymen) are directed, "Speak ye to Archippus." This proves that Scripture belongs to the laity as well as the clergy; and that laymen may profitably admonish the clergy in particular cases when they do so in meekness. Bengel suggests that Archippus was perhaps prevented from going to the Church assembly by weak health or age. The word, "fulfil," accords with his ministry being near its close (<reference osisRef="Col.1.25">Col 1:25</reference>; compare Phm 2). However, "fulfil" may mean, as in <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.5">2Ti 4:5</reference>, "make full proof of thy ministry." "Give all diligence to follow it out fully"; a monition perhaps needed by Archippus.<div eID="gen36566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Lord--</hi>The element in which every work of the Christian, and especially the Christian minister, is to be done (<reference osisRef="Col.4.7">Col 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.39">1Co 7:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.2">Php 4:2</reference>). <div eID="gen36567" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 18. Paul's autograph salutation (so 1Co 16:21 ; 2Th 3:17 ), attesting that the preceding letter, though written by an amanuensis, is from himself. Remember my bonds-- Already in this chapter he had mentioned his "bonds" ( Col 4:3 ), and again Col 4:10 , an incentive why they should love and pray ( Col 4:3 ) for him; and still more, that they should, in reverential obedience to his monitions in this Epistle, shrink from the false teaching herein stigmatized, remembering what a conflict ( Col 2:1 ) he had in their behalf amidst his bonds. "When we read of his chains, we should not forget that they moved over the paper as he wrote; his [right] hand was chained to the [left hand of the] soldier who kept him" [Alford]. Grace be with you-- Greek, "THE grace" which every Christian enjoys in some degree, and which flows from God in Christ by the Holy Ghost ( Tit 3:15 ; He 13:25 )
